Step inside the artist’s world, where paintings, sculptures and objects come together in unexpected ways.

At the time, few could have imagined how deeply computers would come to shape our everyday lives. [⚙️ How do you restore a moving work of art? Outside Moderna Museet on Skeppsholmen stands ”The Paradise” (Le Paradis fantastique) by Jean Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle, one of the museum’s most beloved artworks. Behind the scenes, our Sculpture Conservation team is carrying out one of the most extensive conservation projects in the work’s history. The seven moving machines created by Jean Tinguely are being carefully restored to preserve both their mechanics and the artists’ original vision. In this video, our curators My Bundgaard and Marie Grima take you inside the conservation process and explain what is happening, and why it matters. ”The Paradise” will reopen in spring 2027. 📷 Video: My Matson / Moderna Museet](https://www.facebook.com/100068918481641/videos/1703564680698813/?__so__=permalink&__cft__[0]=AZjKbsKJyMuvN4J4L6sFZUZrPuFly7N4I4Nh4adTe5c9YqVOYEYSr1EcNptyTjjW_9Rrg5yih9sM_xHdOzsAXb4Z5RIwzESIMeExRrerXPmaXnSn2xeaMW4lRY--nG1AUdmx7N_iEkHGB4rML595bg)

[🎨 Tomorrow we open “House of Nisaba” at Moderna Museet. Across the museum, paintings, architectures and imagined worlds are taking shape. Twenty-nine international artists come together in an exhibition where mythology, storytelling, digital culture and contemporary painting collide. Many of the works have been created especially for this exhibition. “House of Nisaba” explores what painting can be today, in a time shaped by endless feeds, fractured narratives and shifting realities. Tomorrow, you can also meet several of the participating artists during a live conversation marathon at the museum. Free admission, drop in throughout the day. The programme will also be livestreamed on our Facebook and YouTube channels. [⚙️ How do you restore a moving work of art? Outside Moderna Museet on Skeppsholmen stands ”The Paradise” (Le Paradis fantastique) by Jean Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle, one of the museum’s most beloved artworks. Behind the scenes, our Sculpture Conservation team is carrying out one of the most extensive conservation projects in the work’s history. The seven moving machines created by Jean Tinguely are being carefully restored to preserve both their mechanics and the artists’ original vision. In this video, our curators My Bundgaard and Marie Grima take you inside the conservation process and explain what is happening, and why it matters. ”The Paradise” will reopen in spring 2027. 📷 Video: My Matson / Moderna Museet](https://www.facebook.com/100068918481641/videos/1703564680698813/?__so__=permalink&__cft__[0]=AZjKbsKJyMuvN4J4L6sFZUZrPuFly7N4I4Nh4adTe5c9YqVOYEYSr1EcNptyTjjW_9Rrg5yih9sM_xHdOzsAXb4Z5RIwzESIMeExRrerXPmaXnSn2xeaMW4lRY--nG1AUdmx7N_iEkHGB4rML595bg)

Title: Yayoi Kusama
Chunks: 36,37,38,39,40,41,42,43,47,48,49,50,51,52,53,54
### Revival: 1980s–2026
[edit]
Kusama c.2004
Kusama's move to Japan meant she had to build a new career from scratch.[[22]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Kusama-2018-22) Her organically abstract paintings of one or two colors (the _Infinity Nets_ series), which she began upon arriving in New York, garnered comparisons to the work of Jackson Pollock, Mark Rothko, and Barnett Newman.

### Revival: 1980s–2026
When she left New York, she was practically forgotten as an artist until the late 1980s and 1990s, when a number of retrospectives revived international interest.[[34]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-MOMABIO-34)_Yayoi Kusama: A Retrospective_ was the first critical survey of Yayoi Kusama presented at the Center for International Contemporary Arts (CICA) in New York in 1989, organized by Alexandra Munroe.[[47]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-48)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
Following the success of the Japanese pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 1993, a dazzling mirrored room filled with small pumpkin sculptures in which she resided in color-coordinated magician's attire, Kusama went on to produce a huge, yellow pumpkin sculpture covered with an optical pattern of black spots.

### Revival: 1980s–2026
The pumpkin came to represent for her a kind of alter-ego or self-portrait.[[49]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-49) The 2.5-metre-wide (8.2 ft) "Pumpkin", made of fiberglass-reinforced plastic, was installed in 1994 on a pier on Naoshima, Kagawa, becoming iconic as her profile grew in the following decades;[[50]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-50) it was reinstalled in 2022 after being destroyed by a typhoon a year earlier.[[51]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-51) Kusama's later installation _I'm Here, but Nothing (2000–2008)_ is a simply furnished room consisting of table and chairs, place settings and bottles, armchairs and rugs;

### Revival: 1980s–2026
however, its walls are tattooed with hundreds of fluorescent polka dots glowing in the UV light.
The result is an endless infinite space where the self and everything in the room is obliterated.[[52]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-52)
_Narcissus Garden_ (2009), Instituto Inhotim, Brumadinho, Brazil
_The Spirits of the Pumpkins Descended into the Heavens_ (2017), National Gallery of Australia, Canberra, Australia
The multi-part floating work _Guidepost to the New Space_, a series of rounded "humps" in fire-engine red with white polka dots, was displayed in Pandanus Lake. Perhaps one of Kusama's most notorious works, various versions of _Narcissus Garden_ have been presented worldwide venues including Le Consortium, Dijon, 2000; Kunstverein Braunschweig, 2003; as part of the Whitney Biennial at Central Park, New York in 2004; and at the Jardin de Tuileries in Paris, 2010.[[53]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-53)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
Kusama continued to work as an artist in her ninth decade. She harkened back to earlier work by returning to drawing and painting; her work remained innovative and multi-disciplinary, and a 2012 exhibition displayed multiple acrylic-on-canvas works. Also featured was an exploration of infinite space in her _Infinity Mirror_ rooms. These typically involve a cube-shaped room lined in mirrors, with water on the floor and flickering lights; these features suggest a pattern of life and death.[[54]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-54) A 1996 residency at Mattress Factory also resulted in two of these rooms being installed, alongside _Dots Obsession_. The two infinity rooms, _Infinity Dots Mirrored Room_ and _Repetitive Vision_, remain on view.[[55]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-55)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
From 2015 to 2016, the first retrospective exhibition in the Nordic countries, curated by Marie Laurberg, travelled to four major museums in the region, opening at Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark and continuing to Henie Onstad Kunstsenter Museum in Norway, Moderna Museet in Sweden, and Helsinki Art Museum in Finland.[[56]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-AD15-56) This major show contained more than 100 objects and large-scale mirror room installations. It presented several early works that had not been shown to the public since they were first created, including a presentation of Kusama's experimental fashion design from the 1960s.[[56]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-AD15-56)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
In 2017, a 50-year retrospective of her work opened at the Hirshhorn Museum in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."). The exhibit featured six _Infinity Mirror_ rooms, and traveled to five museums in the U.S. and Canada.[[57]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-wp.opening-57)[[58]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Broad-58)[[59]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-59)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
In January 2020, the Hirshhorn announced it would debut new Kusama acquisitions, including two Infinity Mirror Rooms, at a forthcoming exhibition called _One with Eternity: Yayoi Kusama in the Hirshhorn Collection_.[[65]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Smithsonian_Institution-2020-65) The name of the exhibit was derived from an open letter Kusama wrote to then-President-elect Richard Nixon in 1968, writing: "let's forget ourselves, dearest Richard, and become one with the absolute, all together in the altogether."[[66]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-66)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
In November 2021, a monumental exhibition offering an overview of Kusama's main creative periods over the past 70 years, with some 200 works and four Infinity Rooms (unique mirror installations) debuted at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art. The retrospective spanned almost 3,000 m 2 across the museum's two buildings, in six galleries and included two new works from 2021: _A Bouquet of Love I Saw in the Universe_, and _Light of the Universe Illuminating the Quest for Truth_.[[67]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-67)
In late December 2022, the Hong Kong's M+ museum opened a retrospective on Kusama's career entitled _Yayoi Kusama: 1945 to Now_. The exhibition, which showed until May 2023, was the largest retrospective of her art in Asia, not including her home country.[[68]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-68)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
The Pérez Art Museum Miami held a showing of Kusama's work. _Yayoi Kusama: Love Is Calling_ was on view and accessible to the public throughout 2024.[[69]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Yayoi_Kusama:_Love_Is_Calling-69)[[70]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-71)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
In 2024, Kusama unveiled a new Infinity Mirror Room titled _Infinity Mirrored Room – Beauty Described by a Spherical Heart_ as part of her solo exhibition _Every Day I Pray for Love_ at the Victoria Miro Gallery in London. The installation featured mirrored spheres suspended within a darkened space, continuing Kusama's exploration of repetition, reflection, and the dissolution of the self through immersive environments.[[72]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-72)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
Kusama died at a hospital in Tokyo, on 14 August 2026 from multiple organ failure, at the age of 97. Her death was announced on 27 August.[[73]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Death_announcement-73)[[74]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-75)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
Kusama struggled with her mental health, suffering from obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) as well as hallucinations and mania. Because of her struggles she took up permanent residence at Seiwa Hospital[ja] starting in 1977. She has stated that starting at age 10 she began to have hallucinations of dots, flower, pumpkins, and patterned fabrics that involved them coming to life and speaking to her and enveloping her, a theme often seen in her later works. She has described this as "self-obliteration" and also that her works involving softer materials and/or colors are a way to process and reduce the intensity of her feelings and experiences.[[76]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-77)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
In her early life Kusama was forced by her mother to spy on her father's infidelity, potentially resulting in her "disgust towards sex". Her mother also attempted to stop her from practicing art, taking away Kusama's art materials in hopes to deter her. Additionally, because she lived in Japan during World War II she was sometimes physically unsafe as well.[[78]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-80)

## Meaning and origins of her work
[edit]
Curator Mika Yoshitake has said that Kusama's works on display are meant to immerse the whole person into her accumulations, obsessions, and repetitions. Kusama's use of infinite and repetitive patterns started as a way to cope with intrusive thoughts related to her mental health, and these ideas later shaped her immersive artistic environments.[[81]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-81) Claire Voon has described one of Kusama's mirror exhibits as being able to "transport you to quiet cosmos, to a lonely labyrinth of pulsing light, or to what could be the enveloping innards of a leviathan with the measles".[[82]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Voon-2017-82)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
[edit]
Kusama c.2004
Kusama's move to Japan meant she had to build a new career from scratch.[[22]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Kusama-2018-22) Her organically abstract paintings of one or two colors (the _Infinity Nets_ series), which she began upon arriving in New York, garnered comparisons to the work of Jackson Pollock, Mark Rothko, and Barnett Newman.
texts.37:
### Revival: 1980s–2026
When she left New York, she was practically forgotten as an artist until the late 1980s and 1990s, when a number of retrospectives revived international interest.[[34]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-MOMABIO-34)_Yayoi Kusama: A Retrospective_ was the first critical survey of Yayoi Kusama presented at the Center for International Contemporary Arts (CICA) in New York in 1989, organized by Alexandra Munroe.[[47]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-48)
texts.38:
### Revival: 1980s–2026
Following the success of the Japanese pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 1993, a dazzling mirrored room filled with small pumpkin sculptures in which she resided in color-coordinated magician's attire, Kusama went on to produce a huge, yellow pumpkin sculpture covered with an optical pattern of black spots.
texts.39:
### Revival: 1980s–2026
The pumpkin came to represent for her a kind of alter-ego or self-portrait.[[49]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-49) The 2.5-metre-wide (8.2 ft) "Pumpkin", made of fiberglass-reinforced plastic, was installed in 1994 on a pier on Naoshima, Kagawa, becoming iconic as her profile grew in the following decades;[[50]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-50) it was reinstalled in 2022 after being destroyed by a typhoon a year earlier.[[51]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-51) Kusama's later installation _I'm Here, but Nothing (2000–2008)_ is a simply furnished room consisting of table and chairs, place settings and bottles, armchairs and rugs;
texts.40:
### Revival: 1980s–2026
however, its walls are tattooed with hundreds of fluorescent polka dots glowing in the UV light.
The result is an endless infinite space where the self and everything in the room is obliterated.[[52]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-52)
_Narcissus Garden_ (2009), Instituto Inhotim, Brumadinho, Brazil
_The Spirits of the Pumpkins Descended into the Heavens_ (2017), National Gallery of Australia, Canberra, Australia
The multi-part floating work _Guidepost to the New Space_, a series of rounded "humps" in fire-engine red with white polka dots, was displayed in Pandanus Lake. Perhaps one of Kusama's most notorious works, various versions of _Narcissus Garden_ have been presented worldwide venues including Le Consortium, Dijon, 2000; Kunstverein Braunschweig, 2003; as part of the Whitney Biennial at Central Park, New York in 2004; and at the Jardin de Tuileries in Paris, 2010.[[53]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-53)
texts.41:
### Revival: 1980s–2026
Kusama continued to work as an artist in her ninth decade. She harkened back to earlier work by returning to drawing and painting; her work remained innovative and multi-disciplinary, and a 2012 exhibition displayed multiple acrylic-on-canvas works. Also featured was an exploration of infinite space in her _Infinity Mirror_ rooms. These typically involve a cube-shaped room lined in mirrors, with water on the floor and flickering lights; these features suggest a pattern of life and death.[[54]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-54) A 1996 residency at Mattress Factory also resulted in two of these rooms being installed, alongside _Dots Obsession_. The two infinity rooms, _Infinity Dots Mirrored Room_ and _Repetitive Vision_, remain on view.[[55]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-55)
texts.42:
### Revival: 1980s–2026
From 2015 to 2016, the first retrospective exhibition in the Nordic countries, curated by Marie Laurberg, travelled to four major museums in the region, opening at Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark and continuing to Henie Onstad Kunstsenter Museum in Norway, Moderna Museet in Sweden, and Helsinki Art Museum in Finland.[[56]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-AD15-56) This major show contained more than 100 objects and large-scale mirror room installations. It presented several early works that had not been shown to the public since they were first created, including a presentation of Kusama's experimental fashion design from the 1960s.[[56]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-AD15-56)

The exhibit featured six _Infinity Mirror_ rooms, and traveled to five museums in the U.S. and Canada.[[57]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-wp.opening-57)[[58]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Broad-58)[[59]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-59)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
In January 2020, the Hirshhorn announced it would debut new Kusama acquisitions, including two Infinity Mirror Rooms, at a forthcoming exhibition called _One with Eternity: Yayoi Kusama in the Hirshhorn Collection_.[[65]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-Smithsonian_Institution-2020-65) The name of the exhibit was derived from an open letter Kusama wrote to then-President-elect Richard Nixon in 1968, writing: "let's forget ourselves, dearest Richard, and become one with the absolute, all together in the altogether."[[66]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-66)

### Revival: 1980s–2026
In November 2021, a monumental exhibition offering an overview of Kusama's main creative periods over the past 70 years, with some 200 works and four Infinity Rooms (unique mirror installations) debuted at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art. The retrospective spanned almost 3,000 m 2 across the museum's two buildings, in six galleries and included two new works from 2021: _A Bouquet of Love I Saw in the Universe_, and _Light of the Universe Illuminating the Quest for Truth_.[[67]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-67)
In late December 2022, the Hong Kong's M+ museum opened a retrospective on Kusama's career entitled _Yayoi Kusama: 1945 to Now_. The exhibition, which showed until May 2023, was the largest retrospective of her art in Asia, not including her home country.[[68]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVr__3RdQdSWTHNc4p02pyOr4lng5BL-AoE-3prj016KMO9bJkNTgooDxpTeiVbu7d5mNPIwYzDoDUKqsjPJYPt9lzwRmcgoHgXyBy_x_imCxhtMILW02TVSGgkfkhYMPz#cite_note-68)

Moderna Museet, Stockholm
ANNIKA ELISABETH VON HAUSSWOLFF
ALTERNATIVE SECRECY
Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff belongs to the generation of Swedish artists who emerged in the early 1990s, inspired visually by postmodernist art and theory. See photographs and objects, spanning from her entire career, in dialogue with a personal selection of works from the Moderna Museet collection.
Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff is born in 1967. She represented Sweden at the 48th Venice Biennale in 1999. Several of her early works relate to the situation of vulnerable women; the theme of violence features frequently, as in her well-known work ”Hey Buster! What Do You Know About Desire?” from 1995. She has elaborated on psychoanalytical themes and also explored sculpture, fabric and installations.
In the exhibition you will encounter photographs and objects spanning from her entire career. She was also invited to make a personal selection from the Moderna Museet collection, which are shown as a separate part of the exhibition and in dialogue with the artist’s own works.
The exhibition is shown at Moderna Museet in Stockholm 23 October 2021–20 February 2022 and at Moderna Museet Malmö 9 April–9 September 2022.
For more information, please visit:
https://www.modernamuseet.se/stockholm/en/exhibitions/annika-von-hausswolff/

# World in My Eyes
Artist Talk Series
25.3–17.4 2026
Stockholm
The artist talk series "World in My Eyes" is back, kicking off with Ibrahim Mahama, followed by Zoe Leonard and Aki Sasamoto. The series is a collaboration between Moderna Museet, Konstfack University of Arts, Crafts and Design, and the Royal Institute of Art, and is hosted by Mötesplats Mariatorget.
*   Admission & Tickets  
*   Ibrahim Mahama  
*   Zoe Leonard  
*   Zoe Leonard
Launched in 2023, “World in My Eyes” is an artist talk series in Stockholm presented through a collaboration betweenKonstfack, Moderna Museet and theRoyal Institute of Art, and is organized by Stockholms Stadsmission’sMötesplats Mariatorget.
Its title drawn from the eponymous 1990s electronic music hit by English band Depeche Mode, the series aims to present artistic perspectives from a wide range of media that are changing the relationship between material processes and socio-political imagination.
In its third season, “World in My Eyes” presents Ibrahim Mahama, Zoe Leonard and Aki Sasamoto. Each artist contributes to both the discursive and formal hybridity of contemporary art at a moment of acute geopolitical volatility and increasing polarization.

# World in My Eyes
## Ibrahim Mahama
### Friday 16 January 2026
Ibrahim Mahama, born in Ghana in 1987, is an artist living and working in Accra, Kumasi, and Tamale, all cities in Ghana. Though he was trained in painting and sculpture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology in Kumasi, Mahama works most often in large-scale installations and architecture interventions. An abiding commitment to textile, collage techniques, and the oral histories of those involved in the construction of the built enviroment complicate the monumentality of his work, contributing to an incisive critique of contemporary global trade networks.
Ibrahim Mahama has had recent solo exhibitions at the Kunsthalle Osnabrück, Germany (2023), Oude Kerk, Amsterdam (2022) and the Frac Pays de la Loire (2022). Mahama’s work was included in the Sharjah Biennial (2023), the International Venice Architecture Biennale (2023), the 35th Bienal de São Paulo (2023), and Documenta 14, Athens and Kassel (2017), among many other international exhibitions. Mahama founded the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art (SCCA), Red Clay Studio, and Nkrumah Voli-ni, all spaces dedicated to exhibitions, research, and community-based learning in Tamale.
Zoe Leonard

# World in My Eyes
## Zoe Leonard
### Wednesday 25 March 2026
Zoe Leonard was born in Liberty, a small town in upstate New York, in 1961 and has been based in New York City for most of her life. Rigorously conceptual, Leonard’s work combines photography, sculpture, and site-specific installation. Her photography considers the conventions of contemporary photographic culture, or the ordering of vision the medium enables.
Leonard was a member of ACT UP and the Women’s Action Coalition and participated actively in AIDS advocacy and queer political movements in New York in the 1980s and 1990s. She is a founding member of the queer artist collective fierce pussy, founded in 1991. Leonard has exhibited widely since the early 1990s, including Documenta IX and Documenta XII, as well as the Whitney biennials in 1993, 1997 and 2014. Her work was the subject of a retrospective exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles in 2018. She presented her landmark decade-long photography project Analogue in a solo exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art and the Museo Reina Sofia in 2015. Other solo presentations have been organized by the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, Kunsthalle Basel, and Vienna Secession.
Aki Sasamoto

# World in My Eyes
## Zoe Leonard
### Friday 17 April
Aki Sasamoto, born in Yokohama, Japan, in 1980, lives and works in Brooklyn. She is an artist who cycles through mediums tailored to each project, including performance, sculpture, video, and dance. Her practice is marked by interdisciplinary collaboration—with scientists, scholars, as well as other artists—and she identifies alternately as performer, dancer, sculptor, writer, and director.
Solo exhibitions of Aki Sasamoto’s work have been presented at the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo (2025), the Queens Museum in New York (2023), Take Ninagawa in Tokyo (2017, 2022), and the Kitchen (2017). Her work was included in the 59th Venice Biennale and the Busan Biennial, both in 2022, as well as the Kochi-Muziris Biennale in 2016, the Gwangju Biennial in 2012, the 2010 Whitney Biennial 2010 and in Greater New York 2010 at MOMA-PS1 in New York, and the Yokohama Triennale in 2008. Sasamoto holds an MFA from Columbia University in New York.

# World in My Eyes

Mötesplats Mariatorgetis a meeting place for conversation, community, exchange of knowledge and networking between people in different life situations, initiated and run by Stockholms Stadsmission.

# World in My Eyes

### World in My Eyes
Launched in 2023, “World in My Eyes” is an artist talk series in Stockholm presented through a collaboration betweenKonstfack, Moderna Museet and theRoyal Institute of Art, and is organized by Stockholms Stadsmission’sMötesplats Mariatorget.
Artists who have participated in previous seasons include Salman Toor, Cecilia Vicuña, Selma Selman, Jonathas de Andrade, Emeka Ogboh, Geo Wyex and Yazan Khalili.

# Conversation on Swedish acquisitions: Matches
13.5 2022
Stockholm
Meet three artists from different generations, who were recently acquired within the framework of the Moderna Museet's major project for the acquisition of new art; “Swedish acquisitions 2021”. Listen to the artists Kristina Abelli Elander, Astrid Kajsa Nylander and Helena Lund Ek in a conversation about feminist art creation and the importance of predecessors and role models.
How do the possibilities of working as a woman and artist differ from the 1970s and 80s to today? How can one find strength and community in creation through networks?
Listen to the artists Kristina Abelli Elander, Astrid Kajsa Nylander and Helena Lund Ek in a conversation about feminist art creation and the importance of predecessors and role models. The conversation takes place in the exhibition “Swedish Acquisitions: Matches”, which opens on May 7, 2022. The exhibition is the second of two group exhibitions that present works from the Moderna Museet’s major project for acquiring new art “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”.
Kristina Abelli Elander started critiquing prevailing gender relations and social orders in her comicstrip-like paintings early on. Astrid Kajsa Nylander’s paintings often take on a surrealist expression departing from female artists’ work. In her work, Helena Lund Ek engages in dialogue with previous generations of artists and her figurative paintings are often about the body and the female experience.
The conversation is mediated by Linda Fagerström, lecturer in Art Theory at Linnaeus University.

# Conversation on Swedish acquisitions: Matches
## Astrid Kajsa Nylander
Astrid Kajsa Nylander received her MFA 2018 in Jutta Koether’s class for painting and drawing at the Hochschule für Bildende Künste Hamburg. In 2019, she was awarded the ‘Junge Kunst’ prize by the Stiftung Sparkasse Siegen, followed by a solo exhibition at the Siegen Kunstverein, Germany. In 2020, her mini-jobs were shown in a solo exhibition at the PAGE Gallery (NYC) in New York. Her solo exhibition “drip drop” opens on May 21, 2022 at Galleri Belenius in Stockholm.

# Conversation on Swedish acquisitions: Matches
## Helena Lund Ek
Helena Lund Ek graduated in 2014 from the Oslo Academy of the Arts and is currently a substitute lecturer in painting at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts. Lund Ek participated in Modernautställningen in 2018 and has since initiated three site-specific solo exhibitions in Stockholm.
Together, Helena Lund Ek and Astrid Kajsa Nylander run Painting Practice, a collegial forum for painting with talks, exhibitions and workshops.

# Conversation on Swedish acquisitions: Matches
13.5 2022
Stockholm
Meet three artists from different generations, who were recently acquired within the framework of the Moderna Museet's major project for the acquisition of new art; “Swedish acquisitions 2021”. Listen to the artists Kristina Abelli Elander, Astrid Kajsa Nylander and Helena Lund Ek in a conversation about feminist art creation and the importance of predecessors and role models.
How do the possibilities of working as a woman and artist differ from the 1970s and 80s to today? How can one find strength and community in creation through networks?
Listen to the artists Kristina Abelli Elander, Astrid Kajsa Nylander and Helena Lund Ek in a conversation about feminist art creation and the importance of predecessors and role models. The conversation takes place in the exhibition “Swedish Acquisitions: Matches”, which opens on May 7, 2022. The exhibition is the second of two group exhibitions that present works from the Moderna Museet’s major project for acquiring new art “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”.
Kristina Abelli Elander started critiquing prevailing gender relations and social orders in her comicstrip-like paintings early on. Astrid Kajsa Nylander’s paintings often take on a surrealist expression departing from female artists’ work. In her work, Helena Lund Ek engages in dialogue with previous generations of artists and her figurative paintings are often about the body and the female experience.
The conversation is mediated by Linda Fagerström, lecturer in Art Theory at Linnaeus University.

The artist talk series "World in My Eyes" is back, kicking off with Ibrahim Mahama, followed by Zoe Leonard and Aki Sasamoto. Launched in 2023, “World in My Eyes” is an artist talk series in Stockholm presented through a collaboration betweenKonstfack, Moderna Museet and theRoyal Institute of Art, and is organized by Stockholms Stadsmission’sMötesplats Mariatorget.
Its title drawn from the eponymous 1990s electronic music hit by English band Depeche Mode, the series aims to present artistic perspectives from a wide range of media that are changing the relationship between material processes and socio-political imagination.
In its third season, “World in My Eyes” presents Ibrahim Mahama, Zoe Leonard and Aki Sasamoto. Each artist contributes to both the discursive and formal hybridity of contemporary art at a moment of acute geopolitical volatility and increasing polarization.

# World in My Eyes
## Ibrahim Mahama
### Friday 16 January 2026
Ibrahim Mahama, born in Ghana in 1987, is an artist living and working in Accra, Kumasi, and Tamale, all cities in Ghana. Though he was trained in painting and sculpture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology in Kumasi, Mahama works most often in large-scale installations and architecture interventions. An abiding commitment to textile, collage techniques, and the oral histories of those involved in the construction of the built enviroment complicate the monumentality of his work, contributing to an incisive critique of contemporary global trade networks.
Ibrahim Mahama has had recent solo exhibitions at the Kunsthalle Osnabrück, Germany (2023), Oude Kerk, Amsterdam (2022) and the Frac Pays de la Loire (2022). Mahama’s work was included in the Sharjah Biennial (2023), the International Venice Architecture Biennale (2023), the 35th Bienal de São Paulo (2023), and Documenta 14, Athens and Kassel (2017), among many other international exhibitions. Mahama founded the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art (SCCA), Red Clay Studio, and Nkrumah Voli-ni, all spaces dedicated to exhibitions, research, and community-based learning in Tamale.
Zoe Leonard
texts.6:
# World in My Eyes
## Zoe Leonard
### Wednesday 25 March 2026
Zoe Leonard was born in Liberty, a small town in upstate New York, in 1961 and has been based in New York City for most of her life. Rigorously conceptual, Leonard’s work combines photography, sculpture, and site-specific installation. Her photography considers the conventions of contemporary photographic culture, or the ordering of vision the medium enables.
Leonard was a member of ACT UP and the Women’s Action Coalition and participated actively in AIDS advocacy and queer political movements in New York in the 1980s and 1990s. She is a founding member of the queer artist collective fierce pussy, founded in 1991. Leonard has exhibited widely since the early 1990s, including Documenta IX and Documenta XII, as well as the Whitney biennials in 1993, 1997 and 2014. Her work was the subject of a retrospective exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles in 2018. She presented her landmark decade-long photography project Analogue in a solo exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art and the Museo Reina Sofia in 2015. Other solo presentations have been organized by the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, Kunsthalle Basel, and Vienna Secession.
Aki Sasamoto
texts.7:
# World in My Eyes
## Zoe Leonard
### Friday 17 April
Aki Sasamoto, born in Yokohama, Japan, in 1980, lives and works in Brooklyn. She is an artist who cycles through mediums tailored to each project, including performance, sculpture, video, and dance. Her practice is marked by interdisciplinary collaboration—with scientists, scholars, as well as other artists—and she identifies alternately as performer, dancer, sculptor, writer, and director.
Solo exhibitions of Aki Sasamoto’s work have been presented at the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo (2025), the Queens Museum in New York (2023), Take Ninagawa in Tokyo (2017, 2022), and the Kitchen (2017). Her work was included in the 59th Venice Biennale and the Busan Biennial, both in 2022, as well as the Kochi-Muziris Biennale in 2016, the Gwangju Biennial in 2012, the 2010 Whitney Biennial 2010 and in Greater New York 2010 at MOMA-PS1 in New York, and the Yokohama Triennale in 2008. Sasamoto holds an MFA from Columbia University in New York.

Moderna Museet, Stockholm
ANNIKA ELISABETH VON HAUSSWOLFF
ALTERNATIVE SECRECY
Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff belongs to the generation of Swedish artists who emerged in the early 1990s, inspired visually by postmodernist art and theory. See photographs and objects, spanning from her entire career, in dialogue with a personal selection of works from the Moderna Museet collection.
Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff is born in 1967. She represented Sweden at the 48th Venice Biennale in 1999. Several of her early works relate to the situation of vulnerable women; the theme of violence features frequently, as in her well-known work ”Hey Buster! What Do You Know About Desire?” from 1995. She has elaborated on psychoanalytical themes and also explored sculpture, fabric and installations.
In the exhibition you will encounter photographs and objects spanning from her entire career. She was also invited to make a personal selection from the Moderna Museet collection, which are shown as a separate part of the exhibition and in dialogue with the artist’s own works.
The exhibition is shown at Moderna Museet in Stockholm 23 October 2021–20 February 2022 and at Moderna Museet Malmö 9 April–9 September 2022.
For more information, please visit:
https://www.modernamuseet.se/stockholm/en/exhibitions/annika-von-hausswolff/

The artist Korakrit Arunanondchai’s interdisciplinary works explore dualities such as life and death, past and present, dream and reality, reflection and rapture, man and machine, individualism and interconnectedness.
In a narrative vein, he fills Moderna Museet with hybridised form of documentary, film, installation, performance, painting and sculpture. Paintings expand into murals, video projections reflect onto water and sweep across the room.
> As the author I exist in between the image and the audience, in the air of the room, telling the story. I am never completely inside one world or another. – Korakrit Arunanondchai
Installation view from Korakrit Arunanondchai – From dying to living, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lundén / Moderna Museet

## Korakrit Arunanondchai
Korakrit Arunanondchai (born in Bangkok, Thailand, in 1986) lives and works in New York and Bangkok. Raised in Thailand, he moved to study in the USA at the Rhode Island School of Design (2009) and Columbia University (2012).
His most recent solo exhibitions have been at the Migros Museum for Contemporary Art in Zürich (2022), Kunsthall Trondheim (2021), Serralves Museum in Porto (2020), the Secession in Vienna (2019), and Kasseler Kunstverein, Kassel (2018).
Arunanondchai’s work has also been presented as part of numerous group exhibitions, and at biennales and festivals, including Mountain/Time at Aspen Art Museum (2022), the Gwangju Biennale (2021), the Yokohama Triennale (2020), and the Venice and Whitney Biennales (2019).

## Korakrit Arunanondchai
### Political and personal
Korakrit Arunanondchai’s practice addresses issues of inbetweenness and dissolved identity with regard to generation, gender and nationality. Animism, natural sciences, philosophy and poetry also play an important role in Arunanondchai’s art, where the power of storytelling is at the core, and the boundary between the personal, the spiritual and the geopolitical is blurred.
Arunanondchai also repeatedly sources material and ideas from conflicts in contemporary Thailand and portrays corrupt belief systems and propaganda from the Cold War in South-East Asia. He interweaves these themes with his own life and family history.
Korakrit Arunanondchai & Alex Gvojic, Installation view from ”Pray” with Korakrit Arunanondchai, 2022 Courtesy Bangkok CityCity Gallery, Bangkok; Carlos/Ishikawa, London; C L E A R I N G, New York/Brussels; Kukje Gallery, Seoul/Busan. Photo: Soopakorn Sirsakul
> Korakrit Arunanondchai’s way of everting the individual’s relationship to the world around them, and upturning hierarchies between the personal, the esoteric, and the political, questions humans’ conditions in other contexts. – Lena Essling, curator

## Exhibition Guide
Hear Korakrit Arunanondchai’s thoughts and ideas on the artworks in the exhibition on our Exhibition Guide.
– The submersion and remersion, the space in between, the motions of falling into and coming out of the water, is where the new work ”From dying to living” comes in: how to connect the two parts, he says in the film.
**Visit the Exhibition Guide: Korakrit Arunanondchai – From dying to living**

## Exhibition Guide
### Collaboration and collectivity
Collaborations and collective work processes are essential to Korakrit Arunanondchai’s practice. Frequent collaborators are the filmmaker Alex Gvojic and the performance artist Tosh Basco, aka boychild.
> The collaboration and the process of making and unmaking are as important as the finished work itself. – Korakrit Arunanondchai

## Exhibition Guide
### New work for Moderna Museet
Korakrit Arunanondchai and Alex Gvojic have produced a new work, “From dying to living” (2022), which is also the title of the exhibition. In this work, the artist explores the threshold between the physical world and the spiritual realm.
“From dying to living” is based on two video works, “Songs for dying” and “Songs for living” from 2021, which constitute opposite poles in the exhibition.
**Visit our Exhibition Guide to hear Korakrit Arunanondchai talk about the artworks in the exhibition.**
Korakrit Arunanondchai, Songs for dying, 2021 (filmstill) © Korakrit Arunanondchai 2021. Courtesy of the artist; Bangkok CityCity Gallery, Bangkok; Carlos/Ishikawa, London; C L E A R I N G, New York/Brussels; Kukje Gallery, Seoul/Busan. Co-commissioned by the 13th Gwangju Biennale, Han Nefkens Foundation and Kunsthall Trondheim
Korakrit Arunanondchai & Alex Gvojic, Songs for living, 2021 (filmstill) © Korakrit Arunanondchai. Co-commissioned by Migros Museum für Gegenwartskunst and Kunstverein in Hamburg with support from FACT, Liverpool

## Exhibition Guide
### Opposites in the exhibition
The video work “Songs for dying” (2021) conflates 2020’s violent popular protests for democratic reform in Thailand with the censored and hushed-up massacre on the island of Jeju in post-war South Korea in 1948.
Central to the work is Korakrit Arunanondchai’s own personal farewell to his grandfather, whose death severs a link to understanding the consequences of the Cold War in this region – and also to the artist’s own family history.
“Songs for living” (2021) is a narrative underpinned by music and words borrowed from the French poet and philosopher Édouard Glissant, the Polish author and Nobel laureate Czesław Miłosz, and the French philosopher, mystic and activist Simone Weil.
Here, Korakrit Arunanondchai and the filmmaker Alex Gvojic together raise questions about affinity and reconciliation with something bigger than ourselves.

## Korakrit Arunanondchai
Korakrit Arunanondchai (born in Bangkok, Thailand, in 1986) lives and works in New York and Bangkok. Raised in Thailand, he moved to study in the USA at the Rhode Island School of Design (2009) and Columbia University (2012).
His most recent solo exhibitions have been at the Migros Museum for Contemporary Art in Zürich (2022), Kunsthall Trondheim (2021), Serralves Museum in Porto (2020), the Secession in Vienna (2019), and Kasseler Kunstverein, Kassel (2018).
Arunanondchai’s work has also been presented as part of numerous group exhibitions, and at biennales and festivals, including Mountain/Time at Aspen Art Museum (2022), the Gwangju Biennale (2021), the Yokohama Triennale (2020), and the Venice and Whitney Biennales (2019).

Moderna Museet in Stockholm held several 2022 exhibitions featuring deceased artists, including a major show of Hilma af Klint’s “The Ten Largest” series in autumn 2022. The museum’s permanent collection also highlights works by Pablo Picasso, Salvador Dalí, Andy Warhol, and Matisse, all deceased modern masters.
Hilma af Klint: The Ten Largest at Moderna Museet
Moderna Museet presented Hilma af Klint’s iconic “The Ten Largest” series in autumn 2022, alongside her watercolours and a complete collection of hand-coloured photographs never shown in full before. Af Klint, who died in 1944, is known for her pioneering abstract works created as part of a spiritual and ritual process.

The museum’s permanent collection includes key works by deceased modern artists such as Pablo Picasso, Salvador Dalí, Andy Warhol, Damien Hirst, Robert Rauschenberg, Francis Bacon, Marcel Duchamp, and Matisse. ## 2022 Moderna Museet Exhibitions Featuring Deceased Artists
While not at Moderna Museet, 2022 saw several notable exhibitions of deceased artists internationally. The Royal Academy in London hosted “Making Modernism” with Paula Modersohn-Becker (1876–1907) and Käthe Kollwitz (1867–1945). The Musée d’Orsay presented “Edvard Munch: A POEM OF LOVE, LIFE AND DEATH” from September 2022 to January 2023, covering the Norwegian painter who died in 1944.
**Studio International** Making Modernism: Paula Modersohn-Becker, Käthe Kollwitz, Gabriele Münter and Marianne Werefkin Royal Academy of Arts, London 12 November 2022 – 12 February 2023 Making Modernism is a jewel of an exhibition. Built around the work of four female artists working in Germany in the early 20th century, this show excels in its intelligent handling of works by Paula Modersohn-Becker (1876-1907), Käthe Kollwitz (1867-1945), Gabriele Münter (1877-1962) and Marianne Werefkin (1860-1938). There are additional works by Erma Bossi (1875-1952), Ottilie Reylaender (1882-1965) and Jacoba van Heemskerck (1876-1923), but Modersohn-Becker and Kollwitz are the stars here, with Münter and Werefkin providing strong parallels. The artist Korakrit Arunanondchai’s interdisciplinary works explore dualities such as life and death, past and present, dream and reality, reflection and rapture, man and machine, individualism and interconnectedness.
In a narrative vein, he fills Moderna Museet with hybridised form of documentary, film, installation, performance, painting and sculpture. Paintings expand into murals, video projections reflect onto water and sweep across the room.
> As the author I exist in between the image and the audience, in the air of the room, telling the story. I am never completely inside one world or another. – Korakrit Arunanondchai
Installation view from Korakrit Arunanondchai – From dying to living, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lundén / Moderna Museet
texts.1:
## Korakrit Arunanondchai
Korakrit Arunanondchai (born in Bangkok, Thailand, in 1986) lives and works in New York and Bangkok. Raised in Thailand, he moved to study in the USA at the Rhode Island School of Design (2009) and Columbia University (2012).
His most recent solo exhibitions have been at the Migros Museum for Contemporary Art in Zürich (2022), Kunsthall Trondheim (2021), Serralves Museum in Porto (2020), the Secession in Vienna (2019), and Kasseler Kunstverein, Kassel (2018).
Arunanondchai’s work has also been presented as part of numerous group exhibitions, and at biennales and festivals, including Mountain/Time at Aspen Art Museum (2022), the Gwangju Biennale (2021), the Yokohama Triennale (2020), and the Venice and Whitney Biennales (2019).
texts.2:
## Korakrit Arunanondchai
### Political and personal
Korakrit Arunanondchai’s practice addresses issues of inbetweenness and dissolved identity with regard to generation, gender and nationality. Animism, natural sciences, philosophy and poetry also play an important role in Arunanondchai’s art, where the power of storytelling is at the core, and the boundary between the personal, the spiritual and the geopolitical is blurred.
Arunanondchai also repeatedly sources material and ideas from conflicts in contemporary Thailand and portrays corrupt belief systems and propaganda from the Cold War in South-East Asia. He interweaves these themes with his own life and family history.
Korakrit Arunanondchai & Alex Gvojic, Installation view from ”Pray” with Korakrit Arunanondchai, 2022 Courtesy Bangkok CityCity Gallery, Bangkok; Carlos/Ishikawa, London; C L E A R I N G, New York/Brussels; Kukje Gallery, Seoul/Busan. Photo: Soopakorn Sirsakul
> Korakrit Arunanondchai’s way of everting the individual’s relationship to the world around them, and upturning hierarchies between the personal, the esoteric, and the political, questions humans’ conditions in other contexts. – Lena Essling, curator
texts.3:
## Exhibition Guide
Hear Korakrit Arunanondchai’s thoughts and ideas on the artworks in the exhibition on our Exhibition Guide.
– The submersion and remersion, the space in between, the motions of falling into and coming out of the water, is where the new work ”From dying to living” comes in: how to connect the two parts, he says in the film.
**Visit the Exhibition Guide: Korakrit Arunanondchai – From dying to living**
texts.4:
## Exhibition Guide
### Collaboration and collectivity
Collaborations and collective work processes are essential to Korakrit Arunanondchai’s practice. Frequent collaborators are the filmmaker Alex Gvojic and the performance artist Tosh Basco, aka boychild.
> The collaboration and the process of making and unmaking are as important as the finished work itself. – Korakrit Arunanondchai
texts.5:
## Exhibition Guide
### New work for Moderna Museet
Korakrit Arunanondchai and Alex Gvojic have produced a new work, “From dying to living” (2022), which is also the title of the exhibition. In this work, the artist explores the threshold between the physical world and the spiritual realm.
“From dying to living” is based on two video works, “Songs for dying” and “Songs for living” from 2021, which constitute opposite poles in the exhibition.
**Visit our Exhibition Guide to hear Korakrit Arunanondchai talk about the artworks in the exhibition.**
Korakrit Arunanondchai, Songs for dying, 2021 (filmstill) © Korakrit Arunanondchai 2021. texts.6:
## Exhibition Guide
### Opposites in the exhibition
The video work “Songs for dying” (2021) conflates 2020’s violent popular protests for democratic reform in Thailand with the censored and hushed-up massacre on the island of Jeju in post-war South Korea in 1948.
Central to the work is Korakrit Arunanondchai’s own personal farewell to his grandfather, whose death severs a link to understanding the consequences of the Cold War in this region – and also to the artist’s own family history.
“Songs for living” (2021) is a narrative underpinned by music and words borrowed from the French poet and philosopher Édouard Glissant, the Polish author and Nobel laureate Czesław Miłosz, and the French philosopher, mystic and activist Simone Weil.
Here, Korakrit Arunanondchai and the filmmaker Alex Gvojic together raise questions about affinity and reconciliation with something bigger than ourselves.

Title: Moderna Museet Announces 2027 Programme
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Moderna Museet has announced details of exhibitions opening during the first half of 2027 in Stockholm and Malmö. Dates are provisional and may be subject to change.More details from the website.
**Remedios Varo
20th February–9th May 2027**
Remedios Varo (1908–1963) was born in Catalonia, Spain, and came to Mexico City as a war refugee in 1941, where she became part of a dynamic network of Mexican artists and surrealists in exile. Her art testifies to a deep engagement with esoteric traditions, such as Gurdjieff’s teachings, Ouspensky’s Fourth Dimension, tarot and alchemy.
Rituals and mysticism are combined with the exploration of new sciences and the subconscious in Remedios Varos’ visionary painting. In her art, a universe of imaginary interiors and landscapes populated by enigmatic figures opens up.
The exhibition is the first retrospective of Remedios Varo in Europe and is organised by the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk, in collaboration with Moderna Museet.
Curator: Lena Essling, Moderna Museet, in collaboration with Mexican art historian Tere Arcq and Kirsten Degel, Louisiana Museum of Modern Art.
_Remedios Varo,_ Still Life Reviving (Naturaleza muerta resucitando)_, 1963. – Artwork Location: Art Institute of Chicago, Chicago (IL), USA_
**Anu Põder
10th April–6th June 2027**
The Estonian artist Anu Põder (1947–2013) explored the fragility and complexity of life and the body in her sculptures. Unlike many of her contemporary colleagues, she worked primarily with plastic, wax, fat and textile – materials that are allowed to live their own lives, change and break down over time.
Spanning three decades, the exhibition traces Anu Põder’s artistic development from the years of Soviet occupation to the period following Estonia’s independence, showing how her focus gradually shifted from the bodily and the ephemeral to commentary on consumerism and capitalism.
Moderna Museet’s exhibition is one of the few solo exhibitions of Anu Põder’s work to be held outside Estonia. In addition to several of her most significant works, it also features drawings that have never been shown before.

The exhibition is a collaboration between Moderna Museet in Stockholm and Moderna Museet Malmö.
Curators: Andreas Nilsson, Moderna Museet Malmö, and Jo Widoff, Moderna Museet, Stockholm
_Anu Põder,_ Kompositsioon mehe peaga (Mehe pea lipuga)/Composition With Man’s Head (Man’s Head with Flag)_, 1984. Photo: Stanislav Stepaško/Art Museum of Estonia © The Anu Põder Estate 2026_
**Claes Oldenburg, Soft Serve
10th April–29th August 2027**
Amidst the overlooked objects and spaces of everyday life, bathroom fixtures, light switches and discarded cardboard boxes, Claes Oldenburg (1929–2022) saw the extraordinary and made it his art. By enlarging, displacing and refashioning everyday items, he transformed the familiar into something soft, pliable and unexpected.
In Soft Serve, visitors follow the trajectory of Claes Oldenburg’s oeuvre, from his early experiments in 1960s New York to the monumental public works that transformed the possibilities of sculpture. This retrospective exhibition returns to an artist who consistently challenged the boundaries between art and life, monument and anti-monument, seriousness and play – and who continues to influence how we perceive the world around us.
The exhibition is organised in collaboration with Kunsthaus Zürich, where it will open later in the autumn of 2027.
Curators: Jo Widoff, Moderna Museet, and Cathérine Hug, Kunsthaus Zürich
_Photo of Claes Oldenburg, by Hans Hammarskiöld, 1966. Moderna Museet. Repro photo: Tobias Fischer/Moderna Museet © Hans Hammarskiöld Heritage 2026_
**Exhibition periods for the current collection exhibitions in Stockholm are being extended.**_The Art of Collecting: Expanding the Moderna Museet Collection_ Closing date: 30th January 2028
_The Subterranean Sky. Surrealism in the Moderna Museet Collection_ Closing date: 28th May 2028
_Will You Be Profitable, My Friend? Swedish Art 1945–1979 in the Moderna Museet Collection_ Closing date: 27th August 2028

### Moderna Museet Malmö
**Ingrid Furre**
**20th March–29th August 2027**
The solo exhibition is the largest institutional presentation to date by the Norwegian, Malmö-based artist and writer Ingrid Furre. The exhibition brings together new works in an extensive installation where sculpture, language, and the body converge.
Ingrid Furre works with materials such as wax, fabric, soap, concrete, wood, and aluminium, creating works that move between the abstract and the everyday. Through a poetic and experimental visual language, she explores the relationship between object, space, and viewer, in environments that feel both familiar and unexpected.
A bilingual publication will accompany the exhibition. Ingrid Furre is represented in the Moderna Museet Collection.
Curator: Andreas Nilsson
The exhibition is shown in the Galleries on Floor 2.
_Ingrid Furre,_ The Blue Sphere _, 2012 © Ingrid Furre/Bildupphovsrätt 2026 Photo: Tobias Fischer/Moderna Museet._
**Portia Zvavahera
14th May–3rd October 2027**Portia Zvavahera paints her dreams. She believes that dreams can help us understand emotions and experiences that disturb and elude us, offering a path through despair, anxiety, and chaos. For Zvavahera, dreams are intimately intertwined with the divine and form the basis of her monumental paintings.
Her colourful canvases are populated by human and animal figures, vegetal motifs, and abstract patterns. Ink painting is combined with graphic printmaking techniques, creating textile-like surfaces that both reveal and conceal. From this dreamlike and spiritually grounded visual world emerge themes of motherhood, care, love, fear, and mortality.
Zvavahera is based in Harare, Zimbabwe. The exhibition at Moderna Museet Malmö marks the artist’s first solo exhibition in Scandinavia.
Curator: Joa Ljungberg
The exhibition is shown in the Turbine Hall.
_Portia Zvavahera,_ Kudonhedzwa kwevanhu (Fallen people)_, 2022 © Portia Zvavahera, courtesy of Stevenson and David Zwirner. Photo: Jack Hems._

Moderna Museet has announced details of exhibitions opening during the first half of 2027 in Stockholm and Malmö. Dates are provisional and may be subject to change.More details from the website.
**Remedios Varo
20th February–9th May 2027**
Remedios Varo (1908–1963) was born in Catalonia, Spain, and came to Mexico City as a war refugee in 1941, where she became part of a dynamic network of Mexican artists and surrealists in exile. Her art testifies to a deep engagement with esoteric traditions, such as Gurdjieff’s teachings, Ouspensky’s Fourth Dimension, tarot and alchemy.
Rituals and mysticism are combined with the exploration of new sciences and the subconscious in Remedios Varos’ visionary painting. In her art, a universe of imaginary interiors and landscapes populated by enigmatic figures opens up.
The exhibition is the first retrospective of Remedios Varo in Europe and is organised by the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk, in collaboration with Moderna Museet.
Curator: Lena Essling, Moderna Museet, in collaboration with Mexican art historian Tere Arcq and Kirsten Degel, Louisiana Museum of Modern Art.
_Remedios Varo,_ Still Life Reviving (Naturaleza muerta resucitando)_, 1963. – Artwork Location: Art Institute of Chicago, Chicago (IL), USA_
**Anu Põder
10th April–6th June 2027**
The Estonian artist Anu Põder (1947–2013) explored the fragility and complexity of life and the body in her sculptures. Unlike many of her contemporary colleagues, she worked primarily with plastic, wax, fat and textile – materials that are allowed to live their own lives, change and break down over time.
Spanning three decades, the exhibition traces Anu Põder’s artistic development from the years of Soviet occupation to the period following Estonia’s independence, showing how her focus gradually shifted from the bodily and the ephemeral to commentary on consumerism and capitalism.
Moderna Museet’s exhibition is one of the few solo exhibitions of Anu Põder’s work to be held outside Estonia. In addition to several of her most significant works, it also features drawings that have never been shown before.
texts.1:
The exhibition is a collaboration between Moderna Museet in Stockholm and Moderna Museet Malmö.
Curators: Andreas Nilsson, Moderna Museet Malmö, and Jo Widoff, Moderna Museet, Stockholm
_Anu Põder,_ Kompositsioon mehe peaga (Mehe pea lipuga)/Composition With Man’s Head (Man’s Head with Flag)_, 1984. Photo: Stanislav Stepaško/Art Museum of Estonia © The Anu Põder Estate 2026_
**Claes Oldenburg, Soft Serve
10th April–29th August 2027**
Amidst the overlooked objects and spaces of everyday life, bathroom fixtures, light switches and discarded cardboard boxes, Claes Oldenburg (1929–2022) saw the extraordinary and made it his art. By enlarging, displacing and refashioning everyday items, he transformed the familiar into something soft, pliable and unexpected.
In Soft Serve, visitors follow the trajectory of Claes Oldenburg’s oeuvre, from his early experiments in 1960s New York to the monumental public works that transformed the possibilities of sculpture. This retrospective exhibition returns to an artist who consistently challenged the boundaries between art and life, monument and anti-monument, seriousness and play – and who continues to influence how we perceive the world around us.
The exhibition is organised in collaboration with Kunsthaus Zürich, where it will open later in the autumn of 2027.
Curators: Jo Widoff, Moderna Museet, and Cathérine Hug, Kunsthaus Zürich
_Photo of Claes Oldenburg, by Hans Hammarskiöld, 1966. Moderna Museet. Repro photo: Tobias Fischer/Moderna Museet © Hans Hammarskiöld Heritage 2026_
**Exhibition periods for the current collection exhibitions in Stockholm are being extended.**_The Art of Collecting: Expanding the Moderna Museet Collection_ Closing date: 30th January 2028
_The Subterranean Sky. Surrealism in the Moderna Museet Collection_ Closing date: 28th May 2028
_Will You Be Profitable, My Friend? Swedish Art 1945–1979 in the Moderna Museet Collection_ Closing date: 27th August 2028

### Moderna Museet Malmö
**Ingrid Furre**
**20th March–29th August 2027**
The solo exhibition is the largest institutional presentation to date by the Norwegian, Malmö-based artist and writer Ingrid Furre. The exhibition brings together new works in an extensive installation where sculpture, language, and the body converge.
Ingrid Furre works with materials such as wax, fabric, soap, concrete, wood, and aluminium, creating works that move between the abstract and the everyday. Through a poetic and experimental visual language, she explores the relationship between object, space, and viewer, in environments that feel both familiar and unexpected.
A bilingual publication will accompany the exhibition. Ingrid Furre is represented in the Moderna Museet Collection.
Curator: Andreas Nilsson
The exhibition is shown in the Galleries on Floor 2.
_Ingrid Furre,_ The Blue Sphere _, 2012 © Ingrid Furre/Bildupphovsrätt 2026 Photo: Tobias Fischer/Moderna Museet._
**Portia Zvavahera
14th May–3rd October 2027**Portia Zvavahera paints her dreams. She believes that dreams can help us understand emotions and experiences that disturb and elude us, offering a path through despair, anxiety, and chaos. For Zvavahera, dreams are intimately intertwined with the divine and form the basis of her monumental paintings.
Her colourful canvases are populated by human and animal figures, vegetal motifs, and abstract patterns. Ink painting is combined with graphic printmaking techniques, creating textile-like surfaces that both reveal and conceal. From this dreamlike and spiritually grounded visual world emerge themes of motherhood, care, love, fear, and mortality.
Zvavahera is based in Harare, Zimbabwe. The exhibition at Moderna Museet Malmö marks the artist’s first solo exhibition in Scandinavia.
Curator: Joa Ljungberg
The exhibition is shown in the Turbine Hall.

# Hilma af Klint
The Ten Largest
22.9 2022–8.1 2023
Stockholm
Meet Hilma af Klint and her series of paintings “The Ten Largest”, when the works are once again on show in the museum in autumn 2022. This time the paintings will be exhibited together with a selection of the artist’s watercolours and a complete collection of hand-coloured photographs of “The Ten Largest” that has never previously been shown in its entirety.

# Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
It was autumn 1907 when the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) began the first canvas in a series that would come to be known as “The Ten Largest”. Working on these ten paintings over a period of just 40 days, the result she produced is one of the most monumental legacies of her artistic output. The series is part of a larger collection known as “Paintings for the Temple”, a mammoth project that the artist had embarked upon two years earlier after experiencing non-verbal cues from the spirit world. The challenge of understanding these messages and finding a visual expression for an invisible reality was to preoccupy Hilma af Klint throughout the rest of her life.
Throughout her life, Hilma af Klint sought the right context for her paintings and only showed them to a limited number of people while waiting for the world to become ready to receive their message. Today, more than a hundred years later, her work is acclaimed all over the world.
Hilma af Klint, De tio största, nr 10, Ålderdomen, grupp IV, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk. Photo: Albin Dahlström / Moderna Museet

# Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
### Evolution and spirit worlds
The sheer size of “The Ten Largest” sets them apart from the artist’s other works. In a gigantic 3.28×2.40 metre format, Hilma af Klint celebrates the four ages of humanity: Childhood, Youth, Adulthood and Old Age.
A central theme in “The Ten Largest”, as in the artist’s oeuvre as a whole, is the notion of evolution. Hilma af Klint, however, seems less concerned about evolution in terms of any physical development from one form of existence to another, and focuses instead on evolution on a spiritual plane.
This reflects an interest in spirituality and theosophy that she shared with many of her contemporaries.

# Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
### Close collaboration with The Hilma af Klint Foundation
Thanks to the close collaboration between Moderna Museet and The Hilma af Klint Foundation, in autumn 2022 visitors to the Museum can renew their acquaintance with “The Ten Largest” by Hilma af Klint, showing in Stockholm for the first time since 2013.
The exhibition also includes a selection of watercolours and a collection of hand-coloured photographs that has never previously been on public display in its entirety.

# Hilma af Klint ### The Ten Largest ### 22.09 2022 – 08.01 2023
The Swedish artist Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) is today seen as a pioneer of abstract art. After studying at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts in the 1880s, Hilma af Klint established herself as a landscape and portrait painter in Stockholm. In the autumn of 1907, she began the first painting in the series _The Ten Largest_.
Hilma af Klint worked on these ten paintings for forty days, producing the most monumental paintings of her entire career. The works are part of the series _Paintings for the Temple_, an extensive project that she had been instructed to complete by spirits two years before. These spirits told her that she would be instrumental in “communicating images to humanity of the life that exists beyond everything”.
At the time theosophical and anthroposophical currents were expanding, and like many artists around Europe, Hilma af Klint shared a great interest in spiritualism and spirituality. She would come to spend the rest of her life trying to understand and give form to this invisible reality. Her images work both within and beyond language. Organic shapes meet abstraction and symbols. The tension between the dualities and their endeavour to achieve wholeness and harmony with one another is a recurring theme. The power of growth is a constant presence. _The Ten Largest_ depicts four phases in a human life: childhood, youth, adulthood and old age. Hilma af Klint is, however, rather more interested in the spiritual and mental development than the physical development.
Throughout her life, Hilma af Klint sought the right con¬text for her paintings and only showed them to a limited number of people while waiting for the world to become ready to receive their message. Today, more than a hun¬dred years later, her work is acclaimed all over the world. Through Moderna Museet’s close collaboration with the Hilma af Klint Foundation, the series _The Ten Largest_ can now, once again, be experienced at the museum.
Matilda Olof-Ors
Curator

268 Hilma af Klint (26 October 1862 – 21 October 1944) was a Swedish artist and mystic whose paintings are considered to be among the first major abstract works in Western art history. A considerable body of her work predates the first purely abstract compositions by Kandinsky, Malevich, and Mondrian. She belonged to a group called “The Five”, a circle of women inspired by Theosophy who shared a belief in the importance of trying to contact the “High Masters”, often through séances. Her paintings, which sometimes resemble diagrams, were a visual representation of complex spiritual ideas. ( wikipedia) Images: from different sources; music: The Sheltering Sky, Ryuichi Sakamoto. A central theme in “The Ten Largest”, as in the artist’s oeuvre as a whole, is the notion of evolution. Hilma af Klint, however, seems less concerned about evolution in terms of any physical development from one form of existence to another, and focuses instead on evolution on a spiritual plane.
This reflects an interest in spirituality and theosophy that she shared with many of her contemporaries.

# Hilma af Klint ### The Ten Largest ### 22.09 2022 – 08.01 2023
The Swedish artist Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) is today seen as a pioneer of abstract art. After studying at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts in the 1880s, Hilma af Klint established herself as a landscape and portrait painter in Stockholm. In the autumn of 1907, she began the first painting in the series _The Ten Largest_.
Hilma af Klint worked on these ten paintings for forty days, producing the most monumental paintings of her entire career. The works are part of the series _Paintings for the Temple_, an extensive project that she had been instructed to complete by spirits two years before. These spirits told her that she would be instrumental in “communicating images to humanity of the life that exists beyond everything”.
At the time theosophical and anthroposophical currents were expanding, and like many artists around Europe, Hilma af Klint shared a great interest in spiritualism and spirituality. She would come to spend the rest of her life trying to understand and give form to this invisible reality. Her images work both within and beyond language. Organic shapes meet abstraction and symbols. The tension between the dualities and their endeavour to achieve wholeness and harmony with one another is a recurring theme. The power of growth is a constant presence. _The Ten Largest_ depicts four phases in a human life: childhood, youth, adulthood and old age. Hilma af Klint is, however, rather more interested in the spiritual and mental development than the physical development.
Throughout her life, Hilma af Klint sought the right con¬text for her paintings and only showed them to a limited number of people while waiting for the world to become ready to receive their message. Today, more than a hun¬dred years later, her work is acclaimed all over the world. Through Moderna Museet’s close collaboration with the Hilma af Klint Foundation, the series _The Ten Largest_ can now, once again, be experienced at the museum.
Matilda Olof-Ors
Curator

[🇳🇴🇪🇸 Two artists. Two visions. One extraordinary encounter. For the first time, the works of Edvard Munch and Pablo Picasso come together in a Munch–Picasso exhibition in Málaga Museo Picasso Málaga. 🖼️ Through more than 100 paintings, drawings and prints, discover how both artists challenged artistic conventions and found new ways to express the complexities of human life. Rather than focusing on questions of direct influence, the exhibition examines the shared themes and concerns that shaped their work: love and desire, illness, death, solitude and existential anxiety. # Hilma af Klint
The Ten Largest
22.9 2022–8.1 2023
Stockholm
Meet Hilma af Klint and her series of paintings “The Ten Largest”, when the works are once again on show in the museum in autumn 2022. This time the paintings will be exhibited together with a selection of the artist’s watercolours and a complete collection of hand-coloured photographs of “The Ten Largest” that has never previously been shown in its entirety.
